objects.label: Actors
objects.text: ST.O.A1 Actors

objects.label: The unit
objects.text: ST.O.A1.1 — Revolution, plot and insurgency as three ways to take power [galula-c01]. Asymmetry of tangible and intangible assets [galula-c02]. The cause [galula-c03]. Population support as the shared objective, gained through an active minority [galula-c04], [galula-c05], [galula-c07]. Political mobilization [mao-c13]. The rural base [wylie-c11]. Strategic culture (no card yet).

objects.label: The system
objects.text: ST.O.A1.2 — Five competitive forces [porter-c01]; barriers to entry [porter-c02]; strategic groups and mobility barriers [porter-c07]. Balancing versus buck-passing as a choice set by structure and geography [mearsheimer-c08]. The offshore balancer [mearsheimer-c05]. One power reshaping the system [kissinger-c01]. Border: the explanatory theory of the international system (offensive realism's five assumptions [mearsheimer-c01]; multipolarity and war [mearsheimer-c09]) is PO.O.A5.1. ST.O.A1.2 uses PO.O.A5.1.

objects.label: Alignment
objects.text: ST.O.A1.3 — Coalition value by marginal contribution (M26) [can_we_win-c14], [negot-c06]. Shapley value: in a transferable-utility cooperative game, it is the unique allocation satisfying efficiency, symmetry, null player and additivity (Shapley 1953; uses MA.B.C4 (91A)). Veto players [advanced-c14]. Triangular diplomacy [kissinger-c08]. Calculated betrayal and exit [can_we_win-c03], [can_we_win-c15], [can_we_win-c20]. Alliance entrapment and abandonment (no card yet). Minimum-winning coalitions as a claim about cabinets are PO.O.A2; ST.O.A1.3 uses PO.O.A2.

objects.label: Agency
objects.text: ST.O.A1.4 — Delegation and mediation as strategic moves [soc-c05]. Career concerns [advanced-c13] (its reputation claim is M10, ST.O.A2.3). Moral hazard under a bonus-plus-fine contract [aos-c11]; the contract theorem is EC.O.A3.1. The succession problem of Realpolitik [kissinger-c06]. Mobilization schedules removing crises from political control [kissinger-c07]. Civil–military relations and delegation to machines (no card yet).

objects.label: The game
objects.text: ST.O.A2 The game

objects.label: Class
objects.text: ST.O.A2.1 — Zero-sum versus mixed-motive as the first diagnosis (M11) [gos-c01], [soc-c03], [can_we_win-c07], [negot-c08]. Payoffs beneath declared positions [can_we_win-c08]. The four 2×2 coordination and anti-coordination games [gos-c15]. Stag hunt as assurance [advanced-c02].

objects.label: Coordination
objects.text: ST.O.A2.2 — Focal points and tacit coordination (M09) [soc-c03], [arms-c05], [negot-c03]. Correlated equilibrium [advanced-c10]. Global games [advanced-c11]. Two-sided markets and tipping [advanced-c16]; the market allocation itself is EC.O.A2.

objects.label: Time
objects.text: ST.O.A2.3 — Reason backward from the end-state (M12) [aos-c01], [gos-c02], [can_we_win-c04], with its experimental limit [gos-c03]. Repetition and the shadow of the future (M10) [gos-c10], [negot-c11], [can_we_win-c12], [advanced-c13]. Rubinstein bargaining [gos-c14]: with two players, alternating offers, an infinite horizon, complete information and discount factors below one, there is a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium with immediate agreement (Rubinstein 1982; uses MA.B.C4 (91A)). Rollback bargaining and outside options [aos-c10]. Grim trigger with forgiveness [negot-c13]. Folk theorem: under infinite repetition, with discount factors close enough to one, any feasible and individually rational payoff can be sustained in equilibrium; for three or more players a full-dimensionality condition is also needed (uses MA.B.C4 (91A)).

objects.label: Strategic moves
objects.text: ST.O.A2.4 — Self-binding commitment (M01) [soc-c01], [soc-c02], [aos-c03], [advanced-c15]. Randomized commitment [soc-c06]. Mixed strategy when predictability is punished [gos-c06]. Issue linkage [kissinger-c09]. The negotiation as a designable tuple; BATNA architecture [negot-c04]. The mechanism-design menu [negot-c05]. Protocol as mechanism design [negot-c07]. Game redesign in business [can_we_win-c10].

objects.label: Purpose and levels
objects.text: ST.O.A4.1 — War as the continuation of policy (M14) [clausewitz-c02], [mao-c06], [wylie-c15], [gray-c01]. The trinity [clausewitz-c03]. Positive and negative purpose [clausewitz-c05]; the object of war [mao-c05]. Strategy as control [wylie-c03], [wylie-c18]; as creating power [freedman-c02]; strategic effect [gray-c03]; nature and character [gray-c04]. The kernel: diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action [gsbs-c01]. Levels: five levels in two dimensions [luttwak-c17]; the technical level is never autonomous [luttwak-c07]; grand strategy as top floor [luttwak-c14]; one fact valued differently at different levels [luttwak-c16]; tactics and strategy as one continuum [freedman_strategists-c07]. Operational art as campaign design (thin; [luttwak-c09]).

objects.label: Point of effort
objects.text: ST.O.A4.2 — Concentration at the decisive point (M13) [clausewitz-c08], [suntzu-c07], [mao-c07], [advanced-c07]. Colonel Blotto: two players divide fixed budgets across battlefields, each won by the larger allocation; its mixed-strategy solution is owned by MA.B.C4 (91A). Centre of gravity (M27) [clausewitz-c11], [wylie-c16]; terrorism read through centre-of-gravity theory [wylie-c19]. Direct and indirect [suntzu-c06]; the indirect approach and its circularity [freedman-c11], [wylie-c13]. Victory as isolation of the insurgent [galula-c06]. Generic strategies and "stuck in the middle" [porter-c03], [porter-c04]. Chain-link systems [gsbs-c05].

Deliberate barbarism as instrument [future_of_war-c19]. Lanchester square law: with aimed fire, homogeneous forces and constant attrition coefficients, fighting strength scales with the square of numbers (uses MA.B.C4 (91A)). Space power and autonomous weapons as means (no cards yet).

Protraction: three stages [mao-c03], the jig-saw pattern [mao-c04], the economics of a protracted campaign [suntzu-c03]. The eight-step area strategy [galula-c09]. Paradoxical logic: good road and bad road [luttwak-c01], specialization defeating itself [luttwak-c05], the oversuccessful Maginot Line [luttwak-c11]. Industry evolution [porter-c08]. objects.label: Signals
objects.text: ST.O.A5.1 — Costly signalling separates types [aos-c04], [negot-c18], [advanced-c13]: a separating equilibrium exists when the signal's cost differs enough between types (uses MA.B.C4 (91A)). Adverse selection [aos-c05], [gos-c07] (as market failure it is EC.O.A2; here it is a counterpart's weapon). Self-selection [gos-c08]. Bayesian persuasion [advanced-c06]. Forecasting as a learnable skill [tetlock-c01], [tetlock-c05], [tetlock-c07], [tetlock-c10], [tetlock-c11], [tetlock-c12], [tetlock-c13]; its limit [tetlock-c15]. Self-defeating prophecy [kahn-c01]. Real decisions are ill-posed [kahn-c11]. Imagined futures as causes; no dominant model of future war [future_of_war-c24], [future_of_war-c09].

Fragile, robust, antifragile [taleb_af-c01]. Mitigate fragility first [taleb_af-c02]. Barbell [taleb_af-c04], [taleb_bs-c06]. Flexibility as a resource (M02) [kissinger-c05], [taleb_af-c05]. warrants.defeaters: Factions hidden by the unitary assumption; selection on successful movements.

warrants.defeaters: Utility not transferable; trust and identity outside the model.

warrants.defeaters: Salience is culture-bound; communication changes the game.

warrants.standard: Backward induction or repeated-game result under stated discounting.
warrants.defeaters: Laboratory evidence against rollback [gos-c03]; finite horizons unravel cooperation.

warrants.defeaters: The ladder metaphor misleads [freedman_strategists-c19]; thresholds shift with technology.

sections.governing_thought: Strategy is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects are five features of the strategic situation: actors, the game, coercion, conduct, and information.
sections.key_line:
- Logic: inductive.
- Plural noun: features (of the strategic situation).
- Dimension: the feature of the strategic situation that the claim explains.
- Order: structural, from who contends to what each side knows.

1. **Actors** (ST.O.A1): who contends, how they align, and whether each can bind itself.
2. **The game** (ST.O.A2): the structure of payoffs and moves, and the moves that reshape it.
3. **Coercion** (ST.O.A3): how a threat of harm, held in reserve, changes another's choice, and how it escalates.
4. **Conduct** (ST.O.A4): how means are applied in time and space to reach a purpose.
5. **Information** (ST.O.A5): what each side knows, believes and can predict, and how that knowledge is contested.

Why this dimension. The Encyclopedia's own protocol forbids retrieval by "a scenario's own vocabulary" and requires retrieval "by structure". Its ten Panel axes are ten questions about features of the situation. They group into these five features without remainder (section 4, Panel table).

Rejected dimensions. The ten theatres mix substrate, method and record. The levels of strategy are a scale on which every mechanism recurs [luttwak-c17]. The medium or service is a substrate [wylie-c14]. Clausewitz's trinity [clausewitz-c03] does not place bargaining or forecasting. Purpose–ways–means reduces to conduct (A4.1).

CONTESTED: coercion could be folded into the game as A2.5, giving four features. It is kept separate for two reasons. Its operative move, a threat held in reserve, has its own mechanisms (M03, M06–M08, M18, M19). It also owes a different warrant: deterrence succeeds through non-events, which the game cell's warrants cannot see.
sections.assignment_rules:
1. **Unit is the claim.** A codex card can hold two claims; each gets its own home. Five cards sit in two Concordance rows and are split by claim (section 11).
2. **Adaptive-other rule.** A claim belongs here only if its truth depends on an opponent, rival or counterpart who reacts. A choice against a non-reacting environment is EC.O.A1 (decision) or MA.B.C4 (operations research). CONTESTED exception: ST.O.A5.3 and ST.O.A5.4 are kept, because the corpus treats markets and nature as environments whose response to exposure is adversarial in effect. Alternative: move both to EC.O.A1.
3. **Threat rule.** If the operative move is a conditional threat to impose cost, the claim is ST.O.A3, whatever the instrument. A move that restructures the game without a threat is ST.O.A2.
4. **Medium rule.** Land, sea, air, space, cyber and the information environment are substrates. Coercion through a medium is A3; force applied in it is A4; information created, stolen or corrupted in it is A5.5.
5. **Level rule.** Tactical, operational, strategic and grand-strategic are a scale, not cells [luttwak-c17]. A claim about the levels themselves is ST.O.A4.1.
6. **Case rule.** A dated event (Cannae, Barbarossa, Cuba 1962) is a case. It is evidence handled by ST.M.B4; its historical truth uses HI.O.A1.
7. **Game rule (from MA and EC).** The theorem is MA, the allocation is EC, the choice of game is ST. Test: does the claim change if the opponent can change the game? If yes, ST.
8. **Politics rule.** Why polities go to war is PO.O.A5.1 (Fearon's bargaining failure). How a party coerces or fights is ST.
9. **Business rule.** The firm's conversion, cost, capital and governance are BU.O.A3. Positioning against rivals who react is ST.
10. **Mind rule.** A cognitive bias as a process is MS. Its exploitation or correction against a counterpart is ST.O.A5.2.
11. **Law and philosophy rule.** Whether a use of force is lawful is LA. Whether it is just is PL. Whether it works is ST.
12. **Artefact rule.** How a weapon or exploit works is EN or CS. What it does to the contest is ST.
13. **No Other.** A strategic claim that will not reduce to one feature is a test of the dimension, not a residual cell.

Proposed edits to other pyramids (recorded, not imposed): BU.O.A3 drops "strategy is the choice of which conversion" in favour of "uses ST.O.A1.2, ST.O.A4.2". PO.O.A5.1 keeps war onset and cites ST.O.A3.1 for deterrence and ST.O.A1.3 for alliance credibility (adopted in p2_PO.md). EC.O.A2 adds "used by ST.O.A2". MS judgement heuristics add "used by ST.O.A5.2".
